q: The part of the universe which we can see is termed the visible universe.
e: This is the definition of the visible universe.

q: The actual universe might be smaller than the visible universe.
e: The actual universe might be bigger than the visible universe.

q: The part we can see is determined by the age of the universe.
e: The age of the universe limits how far we can see.

q: For example, suppose that the universe is $1.38 \times 10^{10}$ years old, as indicated by currently available astrophysical measurements.
e: This is the currently accepted age of the universe.

q: That means the farthest away from the earth that we can see, in any direction, is $4.65 \times 10^{10}$ light year, i.e. the distance light can travel in the time since the universe was formed.
e: This explains the observable limit of the universe.

q: To learn the fundamentals of the universe one needs to study astronomy, astrophysics and cosmology which are three closely related subjects.
e: These are the three main fields for studying the universe.

q: Differences come from the domains and goals of the study of the three fields.
e: This explains how the three fields are distinguished.

q: Astrophysics is the branch of astronomy that deals with the physics of the universe, including the physical properties of celestial objects, as well as their interactions and behavior.
e: This is the definition of astrophysics.

q: Among the objects studied in astrophysics are galaxies, stars, planets, exoplanets, the interstellar medium and the cosmic microwave background.
e: This lists the objects of study in astrophysics.

q: Cosmology studies the universe as a whole and its phenomena at largest scales.
e: This is the definition of cosmology.

q: The difference between Astrophysics and Cosmology is the domain and scale of the study.
e: This clarifies the distinction between the two fields.

q: Astronomy is a natural science that deals with the study of celestial objects, which are any natural bodies outside of the earth's atmosphere.
e: This is the definition of astronomy.

q: Examples are the Moon, the Sun, planets, stars, comets, nebulae, star clusters and galaxies.
e: These are examples of celestial objects.

q: The Earth, our planet is part of the solar system that contains eight planets and the Sun.
e: This describes the composition of our solar system.

q: The Sun is a star and there are many others like it in the universe.
e: This places the Sun in the broader context of the universe.

q: The closest star to our own is called Proxima Centauri, together with approximately $10^{11}$ other stars they make up the Milky Way.
e: This identifies our closest stellar neighbor and the scale of our galaxy.

q: The Milky Way is one of about $10^{11}$ galaxies in the visible universe.
e: This gives an estimate of the number of galaxies.

q: Therefore, the visible universe consists of roughly $10^{22}$ stars.
e: This is the estimated total number of stars in the visible universe.

q: Galaxies cluster into groups; our group is labeled the Local Group and contains about 30 galaxies.
e: This describes the local galactic cluster.

q: The main force holding all of these systems together is gravity.
e: Gravity is the dominant force at astronomical scales.

q: Astronomers have created units of measurement for astronomical distances.
e: This introduces the need for specialized distance units.

q: One of these units is called an Astronomical Unit (AU), the mean distance between the Earth and the Sun, that is, $1.496 \times 10^{8} \text{ km}$.
e: This defines the Astronomical Unit.

q: The light year (ly) is the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year.
e: This is the definition of a light year.

q: One light year is $9.46 \times 10^{15} \text{ m} = 9.46 \times 10^{12} \text{ km}$.
e: This provides the conversion for a light year.

q: One parsec (pc) is the distance to a star that subtends an angle of 1 arc sec (arc second) at an arc length of 1 AU.
e: This is the definition of a parsec.

q: One parsec (pc) is the distance to a star that subtends an angle of 1 degree at an arc length of 1 AU.
e: A parsec is defined by an angle of 1 arc sec, not 1 degree.

q: $1 \text{ pc} = 3.26 \text{ ly}$.
e: This is the conversion between parsecs and light years.

q: $1 \text{ pc} = 206265 \text{ AU}$.
e: This is the conversion between parsecs and Astronomical Units.

q: Astrophysicists and astronomers have theorized that the universe must have originated at a single point of infinite density and finite time then began to expand.
e: This describes the initial conditions of the Big Bang theory.

q: This is known as the Big Bang theory.
e: This names the prevailing theory of universe origin.

q: After the initial expansion, the theory maintains that the universe cooled sufficiently to allow the formation of subatomic particles, and later simple atoms.
e: This describes the sequence of events after the Big Bang.

q: Giant clouds of these primordial elements later coalesced through gravity to form stars and galaxies.
e: This explains the formation of larger cosmic structures.

q: This all began roughly 13.8 billion years ago, and is thus considered to be the age of the universe.
e: This states the accepted age of the universe.

q: The diameter of the visible universe is $8.8 \times 10^{26} \text{ m}$ (28.5 Gpc or 93 Gly).
e: This provides the physical data for the diameter of the visible universe.

q: The volume of the visible universe is $4 \times 10^{80} \text{ m}^3$.
e: This provides the physical data for the volume of the visible universe.

q: The mass (ordinary matter) of the visible universe is $4.5 \times 10^{51} \text{ kg}$.
e: This provides the physical data for the mass of ordinary matter in the visible universe.

q: The density (of total energy) of the visible universe is $9.9 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ (equivalent to 6 protons per cubic meter of space).
e: This provides the physical data for the density of the visible universe.

q: The age of the visible universe is $1.38 \times 10^{10}$ years (or) 13.799 billion years.
e: This provides the physical data for the age of the visible universe.

q: The average temperature of the visible universe is 2.72548 K.
e: This provides the physical data for the average temperature of the visible universe.

q: The contents of the visible universe are Ordinary matter (4.9%), Dark matter (23%), and Dark energy (72%).
e: This provides the composition breakdown of the visible universe.
